faq.a: Fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) need micelles formed by bile and pancreatic lipase; loss of these enzymes reduces absorption.
faq.q: Why does fat malabsorption cause vitamin deficiencies?

faq.a: ORS corrects volume depletion but does not neutralise gastric acid; persistent duodenal acidity still needs antacids or bicarbonate.
faq.q: Can oral rehydration solution replace bicarbonate loss?

faq.a: Yes, it does not interact with antiretrovirals; monitor for allergic reactions.
faq.q: Is pancreatic enzyme replacement safe in HIV patients?

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with chronic alcohol use presents with bulky stools and weight loss – what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Order fecal elastase; low result confirms exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.
How does secretin differ from CCK in regulating duodenal secretions? — Secretin mainly stimulates bicarbonate; CCK stimulates enzyme release and gallbladder contraction.

A patient with HIV on antiretrovirals has steatorrhea; what causes should you prioritize? — Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency from HIV‑related pancreatitis, opportunistic infections, and drug‑induced toxicity.

Why is a proton‑pump inhibitor insufficient to treat duodenal ulcer risk in pancreatic insufficiency? — PPIs reduce acid production but do not replace missing bicarbonate; antacids or oral bicarbonate are needed.

In a low‑resource clinic without fecal elastase testing, how can you screen for pancreatic insufficiency? — Use Sudan‑III stool stain for fat and assess clinical steatorrhea; treat empirically if suspicion high.
What are the dangers of untreated bicarbonate loss in the duodenum? — Persistent low pH damages mucosa, predisposes to ulceration, and impairs nutrient absorption, potentially leading to bleeding.

Explain how tropical pancreatitis differs from alcoholic pancreatitis in presentation and prognosis. — Tropical form occurs in younger, non‑alcoholic patients, often with rapid progression to diabetes; prognosis is poorer due to limited treatment options.
When would you avoid giving oral pancreatic enzymes to a patient? — In active severe pancreatitis with necrosis, enzymes may exacerbate autodigestion; wait until inflammation subsides.
ai.title: Small Intestine Secretions
ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: The small intestine releases enzymes, bicarbonate, and mucus that digest nutrients and protect the mucosa. Understanding regulation and common disruptions guides bedside decisions in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: The duodenum, jejunum and ileum secrete a mixture of pancreatic enzymes, bile‑derived bicarbonate, and intestinal brush‑border enzymes that complete digestion and neutralise gastric acid.

b: CCK → I cells → CCK → pancreas & gallbladder
Vagal afferents sense acidity → reflex increase
sections.p: Enteric hormones (secretin, CCK) and neural reflexes trigger secretion. Secretin mainly stimulates bicarbonate; CCK stimulates pancreatic enzyme release and gallbladder contraction.
Acidic chyme entering the duodenum, fat in the lumen, and osmotic load all modulate hormone release. In low‑resource settings, malnutrition and chronic infections blunt these responses.

t.b: Is duodenal neutralisation adequate? Low values suggest insufficient secretin response or pancreatic insufficiency
Detects exocrine pancreatic insufficiency; <200 µg/g stool is abnormal

sections.p: Failure of secretion leads to malabsorption, steatorrhea and electrolyte loss. Common causes in East Africa include chronic pancreatitis from alcohol, tropical pancreatitis, HIV‑related pancreatic disease, and helminthic obstruction.

b: Low fecal elastase confirms exocrine insufficiency
Co‑existing HIV or TB may worsen malabsorption
sections.p: Patients present with bulky, foul‑smelling stools, weight loss, and abdominal cramps. Recognise when to suspect pancreatic insufficiency versus celiac disease or tropical sprue.

t.b: If unavailable, use Sudan‑III stain as a bedside screen
Detects pancreatic calcifications or ductal dilatation; if not possible, rely on clinical picture

b: Pancreatic insufficiency: low fecal elastase, steatorrhea, normal duodenal mucosa
Celiac disease: villous atrophy, positive anti‑tTG, improves with gluten‑free diet
Bicarbonate loss → duodenal ulcer risk; give H2 blocker if enzymes unavailable
sections.p: Examiners may ask you to differentiate pancreatic insufficiency from celiac disease, to outline management when enzyme replacement is unavailable, or to discuss why proton‑pump inhibitors alone do not correct bicarbonate loss.
